card.chief_complaint: sudden right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath

ask.changes_what: Positive: de-emphasize ACS and work up PE/pneumonia/pneumothorax/pericarditis (exam, CXR, PE risk score). Negative: does not remove PE from the differential.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use pleuritic quality to discharge a patient with possible ACS without an ECG and troponin.
ask.escalation_warning: Pleuritic pain with hypoxemia, tachycardia, unilateral leg swelling or hemoptysis warrants immediate PE work-up; with sudden dyspnea consider pneumothorax.

evidence.citation: Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
evidence.population: Adults with acute chest pain in studies pooled by the RCE review
evidence.reference_standard: Confirmed MI by study criteria (enzymes/ECG) in included studies

evidence.citation: Courtney DM, Kline JA, Kabrhel C, et al. Clinical features from the history and physical examination that predict the presence or absence of pulmonary embolism in symptomatic emergency department patients: results of a prospective, multicenter study. Ann Emerg Med. 2010;55(4):307-315.
evidence.population: 7,940 symptomatic US ED patients tested for PE (12 centers); mean age 49, 67% female
evidence.quote: those with an adjusted odds ratio (OR) greater than 1.5 included non-cancer-related thrombophilia (OR 1.99), pleuritic chest pain (OR 1.53)
evidence.reference_standard: Imaging-confirmed PE or DVT within 45 days
evidence.target_condition: Venous thromboembolism (PE or DVT) in ED patients evaluated for PE

ask.how: Ask whether the pain is sharp and clearly worse with a deep breath, cough or sneeze (not with exertion or palpation), and whether there has been any hemoptysis. Ask separately about onset, exertional relation and positional relief so the pleuritic quality is not conflated with other descriptors.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of pleuritic quality does not exclude PE, pericarditis or pneumonia; PE frequently presents with isolated dyspnea or collapse without pleuritic pain.
ask.pitfalls: Pleuritic pain lowers but does not exclude ACS; no history element alone permits discharge without testing. Patients may label any sharp pain as breath-related unless asked specifically about inspiration.
ask.positive_finding: Pleuritic pain lowers the probability of myocardial infarction (LR about 0.2) and shifts the differential toward pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, pericarditis and pleural disease. In ED patients evaluated for PE it modestly raises VTE probability (adjusted OR 1.5).
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; ask before analgesia if feasible.
ask.rationale: Pleuritic pain would prioritize PE, pneumonia, or pneumothorax over ACS and guide immediate workup.
ask.title: Pleuritic chest pain (sharp, worse with inspiration/cough), +/- hemoptysis

ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

evidence.population: Adults with clinically suspected DVT in cohort studies (mostly outpatient/ED referrals)
evidence.quote: Only malignancy (likelihood ratio [LR], 2.71), previous DVT (LR, 2.25), recent immobilization (LR, 1.98)

evidence.population: Adults with clinically suspected DVT in cohort studies
evidence.quote: it stratified patients into groups with high (LR, 5.2), intermediate, and low (LR, 0.25) probability of DVT
evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis (imaging-confirmed), Wells score high vs low category

evidence.citation: Wells PS, Owen C, Doucette S, Fergusson D, Tran H. Does this patient have deep vein thrombosis? JAMA. 2006;295(2):199-207.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results (post-test prevalence by Wells category; no sens/spec/LR)
evidence.population: Consecutive unselected outpatients with suspected DVT, 14 studies (>8000 patients)
evidence.quote: prevalence of DVT in the low, moderate, and high clinical probability groups was 5.0% (95% CI, 4.0%-8.0%), 17% (95% CI, 13%-23%), and 53%
evidence.target_condition: Deep vein thrombosis, prevalence by Wells clinical probability category

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: VTE risk factors would increase suspicion for PE and change the urgency and type of imaging needed.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

examine.changes_what: Unilateral absence after chest trauma or with hypotension: treat as pneumothorax/hemothorax until imaged (POCUS/CXR); with dullness, evaluate for effusion or consolidation.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay decompression of a clinically obvious tension pneumothorax to complete the exam.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on auscultation alone to exclude pneumothorax in an unstable trauma patient or before positive-pressure ventilation; use POCUS or CXR.
examine.escalation_warning: Unilateral absent breath sounds with hypotension, distended neck veins or tracheal deviation is tension physiology: decompress immediately, do not wait for imaging.

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.location: Table 3, row 'Abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds - (Hemato) pneumothorax'
evidence.population: Adults with blunt or penetrating chest trauma (5 studies; abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds)

evidence.citation: Arts L, Lim EHT, van de Ven PM, Heunks L, Tuinman PR. The diagnostic accuracy of lung auscultation in adult patients with acute pulmonary pathologies: a meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2020;10:7347.
evidence.location: Table 3, row 'Abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds - Pneumonia'
evidence.population: Adults with acute respiratory symptoms or suspected pneumonia (6 studies; abnormal, decreased or absent breath sounds)

examine.how: Auscultate both hemithoraces at matched anterior, lateral and posterior points during quiet then deep breathing, comparing each site directly with its mirror-image contralateral site. Note whether breath sounds are absent, markedly reduced or merely asymmetric, and check tracheal position in the suprasternal notch.
examine.negative_finding: Symmetric, normal-intensity vesicular breath sounds bilaterally; this lowers but does not exclude small pneumothorax, effusion or pneumonia.
examine.pitfalls: Sounds transmit across the mediastinum and the finding is insensitive (pooled sensitivity around 0.5-0.7), so a normal exam cannot rule out pneumothorax. Obesity, COPD hyperinflation, shallow breathing and noisy resuscitation bays reduce reliability.
examine.positive_finding: Breath sounds clearly absent or much reduced on one side compared with the other, with or without hyperresonance (pneumothorax) or dullness (effusion/consolidation).
examine.prerequisites: Quiet room, skin contact (not through clothing), patient able to breathe on request; in trauma, examine during primary survey with the patient supine.
examine.rationale: Unilateral absent breath sounds would rapidly point toward pneumothorax or large effusion, prompting urgent imaging or intervention.
examine.title: Unilaterally absent or markedly reduced breath sounds (+/- tracheal deviation as late tension sign)

examine.changes_what: RR >24 with fever/cough: image for pneumonia and assess severity. Normal vitals in low-risk cough: CXR may be deferred. Unexplained tachypnea: check gas/lactate for acidosis.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal RR to exclude PE, sepsis or acidosis; do not rely on charted (estimated) rates.
examine.escalation_warning: RR >=30, or RR >=22 with altered mentation or SBP <=100 (qSOFA >=2), or tachypnea with rising PCO2/fatigue: escalate to higher level of care.

evidence.citation: Htun TP, Sun Y, Chua HL, Pang J. Clinical features for diagnosis of pneumonia among adults in primary care setting: A systematic and meta-review. Sci Rep. 2019;9:7600.
evidence.location: Table 2 (PMC6527561 full text); footnote ¥ gives thresholds
evidence.population: Adults with respiratory symptoms in primary care, no serious illness; 6 studies, n=4,468
evidence.target_condition: Radiographic community-acquired pneumonia (respiratory rate >=20/min; >=22 in one study, >=24 in two)

evidence.citation: Ebell MH, Chupp H, Cai X, Bentivegna M, Kearney M. Accuracy of Signs and Symptoms for the Diagnosis of Community-acquired Pneumonia: A Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(7):541-553.
evidence.population: Adults with suspected pneumonia or acute cough; 17 prospective cohorts (9 primary care, 7 ED)
evidence.quote: it is decreased most by the absence of abnormal vital signs (LR- = 0.25, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.48)
evidence.target_condition: Community-acquired pneumonia (absence of ANY abnormal vital sign, composite including respiratory rate)

examine.how: Count chest-wall excursions for a full 60 seconds while the patient is at rest and unaware (e.g., while appearing to take the pulse). Do not use the triage estimate or a 15-second count multiplied; record the pattern (deep Kussmaul vs shallow rapid) as well as the rate.
examine.negative_finding: A normal rate lowers but does not exclude pneumonia (LR- 0.77); absence of any vital-sign abnormality lowers CAP probability more strongly (LR- 0.25).
examine.pitfalls: Recorded rates are often estimated rather than counted, clustering at 18-20. Pain, anxiety, fever and hypoxia raise the rate nonspecifically; PE frequently presents with RR >20 but the finding is not discriminating.
examine.positive_finding: RR above threshold raises the probability of radiographic pneumonia (pooled LR+ 3.5 for RR >=20-24) and is a qSOFA/CURB-65 criterion; deep regular tachypnea points to metabolic acidosis or uremia.
examine.prerequisites: Patient at rest for several minutes; not talking.
examine.rationale: Tachypnea would indicate severity and need for urgent intervention or escalation of care.
examine.title: Respiratory rate >24-25/min counted for 60 s

examine.changes_what: Positive: adds 1 Wells point and pushes toward compression ultrasound; negative does not stop work-up if other Wells items or D-dimer are positive.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm calf compression if DVT is strongly suspected and pain is severe.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative calf measurement to withhold imaging in a patient with moderate/high Wells probability or with symptoms suggesting PE.
examine.escalation_warning: Massive swelling with cyanosis or pallor and pain (phlegmasia) or a cold pulseless limb requires immediate vascular imaging and consultation.

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: the value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Patients with clinically suspected DVT (cohort studies comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard; pooled random-effects)
evidence.quote: malignancy (likelihood ratio [LR], 2.71), previous DVT (LR, 2.25), recent immobilization (LR, 1.98), difference in calf diameter (LR, 1.80)
evidence.reference_standard: Venography or compression/duplex ultrasound (study-specific reference standard)
evidence.target_condition: DVT (finding: difference in calf diameter, present)

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: the value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Patients with clinically suspected DVT (cohort studies comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard; pooled random-effects)
evidence.quote: absence of calf swelling (LR, 0.67) or difference in calf diameter (LR, 0.57) was useful for ruling out DVT
evidence.reference_standard: Venography or compression/duplex ultrasound (study-specific reference standard)
evidence.target_condition: DVT (finding: difference in calf diameter, absent)

evidence.citation: Goodacre S, Sutton AJ, Sampson FC. Meta-analysis: the value of clinical assessment in the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis. Ann Intern Med. 2005;143(2):129-139.
evidence.population: Patients with clinically suspected DVT (cohort studies comparing clinical assessment with a reference standard; pooled random-effects)
evidence.quote: absence of calf swelling (LR, 0.67) or difference in calf diameter (LR, 0.57) was useful for ruling out DVT
evidence.reference_standard: Venography or compression/duplex ultrasound (study-specific reference standard)

examine.how: With the patient supine and legs relaxed, mark a point 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on each leg and measure calf circumference with a tape at the same level bilaterally. A difference >3 cm (symptomatic side larger) is positive; also note localized tenderness along the deep venous system and pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg.
examine.negative_finding: No calf-diameter difference (LR- 0.57) or no calf swelling (LR- 0.67) lowers the probability of DVT only modestly; it cannot exclude DVT on its own.
examine.pitfalls: Chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema, cellulitis, Baker cyst, and prior DVT produce asymmetry without acute thrombosis; measuring at different levels or in a dependent leg creates spurious differences. Calf tenderness alone has LR near 1.
examine.positive_finding: Calf-diameter difference roughly doubles the odds of DVT (pooled LR+ 1.8); it is the only physical sign with useful rule-in value but is far weaker than the overall Wells score (high probability LR 5.2).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs accessible and comparable (no prior amputation, cast, or chronic unilateral disease that already explains asymmetry).
examine.rationale: Unilateral leg swelling would support DVT as a source for PE, influencing diagnostic and treatment decisions.
examine.title: Unilateral leg swelling: calf circumference difference >3 cm (10 cm below tibial tuberosity), with calf tenderness

examine.changes_what: SBP <90/MAP <65: resuscitate, lactate, POCUS (RUSH) to classify shock type, cause-directed therapy now. Normal BP: keep looking for compensated shock (HR, lactate, mentation, urine output).
examine.contraindications: Avoid the arm with a dialysis fistula, lymphoedema or recent axillary surgery; none otherwise.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a single normal cuff reading to exclude shock or tamponade; do not interpret SBP <90 as 'baseline' without documented prior values.
examine.escalation_warning: SBP <90 or MAP <65 with altered mentation, lactate >2, oliguria or cool skin is shock: immediate resuscitation and senior/ICU review; in suspected dissection or tamponade, hypotension signals imminent collapse.

evidence.citation: Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical examination for acute aortic dissection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2019.
evidence.population: Pooled 4 studies of ED patients evaluated for suspected acute aortic dissection (review total 9 studies, 2,400 participants; prevalence range 21.9-76.1%)
evidence.reference_standard: Acute aortic dissection confirmed by imaging, surgery or autopsy per primary studies
evidence.target_condition: Acute aortic dissection; finding = hypotension as defined by each primary study (thresholds varied; not uniformly SBP <90 mmHg)

evidence.citation: Drazner MH, Hellkamp AS, Leier CV, Shah MR, Miller LW, Russell SD, Young JB, Califf RM, et al. Value of clinician assessment of hemodynamics in advanced heart failure: the ESCAPE trial. Circ Heart Fail. 2009.
evidence.location: Table 5 (Utility of history and physical examination in detecting an invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2); columns frequency, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, LR+, LR-, OR, P
evidence.population: 188 patients hospitalised with advanced decompensated HF in the ESCAPE trial with pulmonary artery catheter measurements
evidence.reference_standard: Invasively measured cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 by pulmonary artery catheter
evidence.target_condition: Low cardiac index <2.3 L/min/m2 in advanced heart failure; finding = SBP <90 mmHg on baseline examination

evidence.citation: Guberman BA, Fowler NO, Engel PJ, Gueron M, Allen JM. Cardiac tamponade in medical patients. Circulation. 1981.
evidence.population: 56 medical patients with cardiac tamponade, single-centre case series, University of Cincinnati
evidence.quote: heart sounds were diminished in 19 patients; arterial systolic pressure was greater than or equal to 100 mm Hg in 35
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/haemodynamic diagnosis of tamponade with relief by pericardiocentesis or pericardial resection
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac tamponade (sensitivity only); finding = systolic BP <100 mmHg (threshold differs from id title's <90)

examine.how: Measure with a correctly sized cuff on a supported arm (manual if the automated reading is doubtful or the pulse is irregular), repeat, and measure both arms when dissection is possible; calculate MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP)/3. Interpret against the patient's usual pressure and drug list.
examine.negative_finding: A normal SBP does not exclude shock (compensated haemorrhage, early sepsis, cardiogenic shock with vasoconstriction) or tamponade (about 60% of tamponade patients had SBP ≥100), nor low cardiac index in heart failure (SBP <90 sensitivity 12%).
examine.pitfalls: Chronic hypertensives are hypoperfused at 'normal' pressures; beta-blockers, pacemakers and automated cuffs in AF mislead. Interarm difference >20 mmHg raises dissection concern. Cuff readings overestimate true pressure in profound vasoconstriction.
examine.positive_finding: SBP <90 (or MAP <65) is shock until proven otherwise and should trigger a search for the cause (septic, hypovolaemic/haemorrhagic, cardiogenic, obstructive: tamponade/PE/tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, adrenal). In suspected dissection, hypotension roughly triples the odds (LR+ 2.9, specificity 95%). It is not a discriminator between causes.
examine.prerequisites: Appropriate cuff size; awareness of baseline BP, beta-blockers/antihypertensives and pacing.
examine.rationale: Hypotension would indicate hemodynamic instability, requiring immediate resuscitation and prioritizing life-threatening causes.
examine.title: Systolic BP <90 mmHg (or MAP <65) at the bedside
